stories.topic: Why dehydration makes cardio harder, and how to use it
stories.summary: An adult has about six litres of blood. Sweat out a litre during exercise and you have lost roughly a sixth of that base, so the blood thickens and the heart works harder to pump it. That is why dehydrated exercise feels so draining and why a drink of water brings quick relief. Ajay's twist: on a treadmill with a fridge of water nearby, you could train slightly under-hydrated on purpose to raise the load on your heart. Amit, who once read 20 to 40 running books in a couple of months, added that marathon runners have died from drinking too much water.
stories.insight: Knowing the mechanism (blood viscosity and pump load) explains a familiar feeling and suggests a training tool. The marathon point is the counterweight: more water is not always better.
stories.quote: So the blood becomes thicker. When the blood is thicker, it is harder for the heart to pump that blood.

stories.topic: The CPAP machine that fixed the wrong problem
stories.summary: Amit tested positive for mild sleep apnea and began using a CPAP machine. Poor sleep had never really troubled him, but chronic acid reflux had: for years he woke most mornings with a cold or a sore throat. The pressurised air from a nasal mask stopped the acid from rising at night, and the morning sore throats disappeared. He also urges anyone who snores to get tested for sleep apnea.
stories.insight: Interventions have second-order effects. The biggest benefit of a treatment can turn up somewhere you weren't looking.
stories.quote: using the CPAP machine for the sleep apnea actually changed that because the air that is gushing into your lungs, especially if you use a nasal mask, prevents the acid from coming up.

stories.topic: Escaping a perfect home office for Starbucks
stories.summary: Amit records episodes in batches (eight episodes in nine days in Delhi, for instance), which leaves him weeks of free time. He admits he wastes much of it on online bullet chess, even in a home office he loves, with a sit-stand desk and all the tech. His fix is to work from Starbucks, where sitting among other people with laptops makes him too sheepish to play chess for an hour.
stories.insight: Discipline is often about designing your environment, not summoning willpower. Even people who look very productive are fighting the same battle.
stories.quote: if you actually go to Starbucks and you're sitting with a laptop, you feel a little sheepish about oh, you know, playing chess for an hour.

stories.topic: A chess rating as a gauge of mental sharpness
stories.summary: Amit has been prescribed modafinil for sleep apnea and uses it, with caveats, during long recording runs. He noticed that on keto, or on days he takes modafinil, his Chess.com bullet rating rises about 100 points, and falls back when he stops. He isn't trying to improve at chess, so the swing works as a fairly clean measure of his cognitive state.
stories.insight: A skill you practise every day can double as a personal experiment that shows how diet and other factors affect your thinking.
stories.quote: when I'm on keto or on days when I take modafinil, I don't take it every day, my ELO rating on chess dot com goes up by a hundred points. And when I come off it comes down by a hundred points.

stories.topic: Two books from Lant Pritchett that changed Ajay's thinking
stories.summary: Lant Pritchett pointed Ajay to Seeing Like a State and to The Functions of the Executive, a 1938 management book that reshaped how he thinks about organisations, both firms and government bodies. Ajay took the suggestions seriously because he respected Lant. Seeing Like a State led him to read everything by James C. Scott, including Against the Grain, which he considers a near-perfect book.
stories.insight: Good books often reach you through trusted people. Spend time with people who know great books, and when someone you respect recommends one, give it a proper chance.
stories.quote: gentle reader, hang out with people who know great books. But second, I respected Lant. I took his word seriously, so I gave these books a serious chance.

stories.topic: 'When are you most happy?' at a café in Bir
stories.summary: Sitting in a café in Bir with Ajay, Vaishnav, Nomsita and friends, Amit asked everyone when they were happiest. One said in the mountains, another said with her dog, and Ajay said when he has a new idea. Amit noticed that every answer was easy to achieve.
stories.insight: Tie happiness to small processes you can reach every day, not to big goals. Big goals are elusive, and even reaching them may not satisfy you.
stories.quote: people often make the mistake of defining happiness in terms of grand goals. And I think those are dangerous, those are elusive

stories.topic: Vinay Singhal's two language struggles, and STAGE
stories.summary: Vinay Singhal grew up in a Haryana village speaking Haryanvi. He had to work hard twice: once to learn English after joining an English-medium school in the eighth standard (he rose to the top of his class), and again to master Hindi when he moved to a city. His venture STAGE now makes content in dialects like Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and Maithili.
stories.insight: Two forces pull on Indian languages. A 'great flattening' pushes dialects toward Hindi and English, while the internet lets niche languages survive on small, devoted audiences. Amit's advice to new podcasters: if your other language is nearly as good as your English, use it, because that audience is underserved.
stories.quote: where you can have niche content with a thousand true fans because every dialect will at least have a thousand true fans.

stories.topic: Hanging off a mountain: 'Let's solve this'
stories.summary: On the hike where Ajay broke his leg, he slipped off an edge and was left hanging while his friend Ayush held his hand. Ajay was soaked in panic sweat. For about thirty seconds, neither said a word. Then Ajay looked up and said, 'Let's solve this.'
stories.insight: This is Ajay's crisis rule in action, which he states elsewhere in the episode: the bigger the crisis, the calmer you need to be, so that you can actually think.
stories.quote: And then Ajay looked up at Ayush and said, Let's solve this. So that's Ajay Shah for you.

stories.topic: Why coming back from America was his best decision
stories.summary: Asked whether he regrets leaving the US, Ajay calls returning to India one of the best decisions of his life. In America he would have worked on second-order problems. In India he got to take on the big founding questions of a developing country and play a small part in important national stories.
stories.insight: Early-stage environments offer outsized purpose. Being a bit player in a big story can matter more than being a star in a mature one.
stories.quote: In America I would have been doing second order stuff. In India I got to do first order stuff.

stories.summary: For years Ajay wore a uniform copied from economists Kirit Parikh and Shekhar Shah: plain white or off-white Khadi Emporium shirts, half-sleeved because India is too hot for full sleeves. He has never worn a suit and tie in India. Later he found printed shirts in Udaipur, tried them on Everything is Everything, liked how they looked, and now most of his shirts are gifts. Many are silk shirts from Indian Colours printed with contemporary Indian art.
stories.insight: A small story about letting go of convention and experimenting late. Signature styles can come about by accident.
stories.quote: Most of my shirts are actually gifts.

stories.topic: How long-form conversations made Amit a better listener
stories.summary: The Seen and the Unseen evolved from short takes on single subjects, to three- and four-hour dives into whole fields, to deep dives into people that sometimes run six to eight hours. Amit says this change in form changed him. He listens to understand rather than to respond, keeps his ego out, and enjoys learning what shaped his guests, including their dreams and fears.
stories.insight: Form shapes the person doing the work. Long conversation demands humility and real attention, and over time it builds both.
stories.quote: a five hour conversation is not five times a one hour conversation. It is a different beast entirely.

stories.topic: From Amul Tetra Paks to protein powder
stories.summary: Having seen how badly Bombay handles its trash, and knowing that plastic breaks down into microplastics that end up in our stomachs, Ajay changed small habits. He buys milk in pouches rather than Tetra Paks, because a pouch uses fewer grams of plastic per litre. After about ten Amul Tetra Pak protein drinks he felt bad about so much packaging for 200 ml, and switched to protein powder.
stories.insight: When the state fails at waste management, small personal choices are a way of living by your values, even if you are a drop in the ocean.
stories.quote: after the tenth of these tetra packs, I just started feeling bad that so much plastic for stupid two hundred ml of the drink, so then I switched to protein powders instead.

recommendations.creator: Ingmar Bergman
recommendations.context: Mid-episode pick, right after Ajay's joke that a country's films get better as its median age rises.
recommendations.reason: Amit thinks it is the best way into Bergman, who can feel inaccessible. It is a masterpiece about old age and growing old gracefully.

recommendations.context: Part of Amit's answer to a request for his top-ten bookshelf. He laments that there is no single primer on classical liberalism.
recommendations.reason: Excellent short introductions to great thinkers he believes everyone should read.

recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: Listed by Amit on his bookshelf and named by Ajay as one of the books that arrived at exactly the right time, via Lant Pritchett.
recommendations.reason: It chipped away at Ajay's belief in technological high modernism. In his words, it showed him 'what a book can do'.

recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: After Seeing Like a State, Ajay read everything else Scott wrote.
recommendations.reason: He calls it one of the most perfect executions of a book. Anyone who wants to learn the craft of writing a book should study it.

recommendations.creator: Chester Barnard
recommendations.context: A 1938 management book that Lant Pritchett recommended to Ajay.
recommendations.reason: It opened up his thinking on organisational behaviour and on what goes wrong in large, complex organisations, both firms and government.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: On Amit's short bookshelf list.
recommendations.reason: Amit simply loves Orwell's essays. He pairs this with a broader plea to read plenty of fiction and watch good cinema.

recommendations.creator: Alain Bertaud
recommendations.context: Added quickly to the bookshelf answer.
recommendations.reason: A masterpiece for anyone who wants to understand cities and urban planning.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked for the question about the ideal human population of the earth.
recommendations.reason: It sets out his 'people are brains, not stomachs' argument against fears of overpopulation.

recommendations.item: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: A video Amit links while explaining why India lost the garment industry to Bangladesh.
recommendations.reason: It makes clear that a minimum wage prices the poorest workers out of jobs entirely, hurting the people it claims to protect.

recommendations.creator: Bjorn Lomborg
recommendations.context: Cited in the answer on degrowth and sustainability, along with Lomborg's work in general.
recommendations.reason: Lomborg traces how great Western cities like London were filthy and unhealthy about a hundred years ago and cleaned up as they got richer. Amit's takeaway: growth helps sustainability.

recommendations.item: Saumya Roy's book on the trash mountains of Bombay
recommendations.creator: Saumya Roy
recommendations.context: Mentioned while explaining why he tries to create less trash.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it amazing. It shows how badly Bombay handles its waste, which is why he avoids plastic.

recommendations.creator: Dan Carlin
recommendations.context: A listener asked for his favourite podcasts.
recommendations.reason: He calls it quite amazing.

recommendations.creator: Sam Harris
recommendations.context: Favourite podcasts.
recommendations.reason: He recommends it for the art of conversation. He loved its flow and rhythm in the early days, though it is now mostly paywalled.

recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: His top Indian podcast pick.
recommendations.reason: He thinks she does an incredible job.

recommendations.creator: Milan Vaishnav
recommendations.context: Favourite podcasts. Vaishnav had been especially active during the elections.
recommendations.reason: Vaishnav is a fine thinker, and the podcast is a good way to follow Indian politics.

recommendations.creator: Milan Vaishnav
recommendations.context: Mentioned along with Vaishnav's podcast.
recommendations.reason: A must-read on crime in Indian politics.

recommendations.creator: Russ Roberts
recommendations.context: Roberts is another favourite and came on The Seen and the Unseen to talk about conversation.
recommendations.reason: A long-time favourite of Amit's.

recommendations.creator: Tony Joseph
recommendations.context: In the answer on how much caste still shapes success.
recommendations.reason: It explains how caste endogamy took hold about 2,000 years ago, after millennia of intermingling, which helps explain why caste runs so deep.

recommendations.item: Who We Are and How We Got Here
recommendations.creator: David Reich
recommendations.context: Paired with Early Indians in the caste answer.
recommendations.reason: Source of Amit's favourite line: India is not one large population like the Han Chinese but a collection of thousands of small ones.

recommendations.item: Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Raised when discussing reservations, which Amit says he is neither for nor against.
recommendations.reason: It asks whether such policies actually helped the people they were meant to help. Amit believes growth helps far more.

recommendations.creator: Peggy Mohan
recommendations.context: A pointer for the question on how Indian languages will evolve. Amit also recorded an episode with her.
recommendations.reason: A great book on the history of India's languages.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: In his answer to Milton Friedman's claim that a business's responsibility is to maximise profit. He recalls writing a column titled 'Profit is not a dirty word'.
recommendations.reason: In a competitive market, profit is earned only by making someone else better off, which makes it the highest form of philanthropy.

recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik, Abhijit Sen Gupta, Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's co-authored paper, cited in the question about whether crypto can increase freedom in India.
recommendations.reason: It shows how Indian businesses misinvoiced trade on a large scale to get around exchange controls and achieve de facto convertibility. In that light, crypto is just one more tool, not something fundamental.

recommendations.item: Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance
recommendations.creator: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck
recommendations.context: His answer to the biggest mistake parents make.
recommendations.reason: Children praised for being smart later tried less and even cheated. Children praised for effort kept trying.

recommendations.creator: Luke Burgis
recommendations.context: On how to approach starting a family and building a life. Amit also recorded an episode with Burgis.
recommendations.reason: It explains mimetic desire, the habit of wanting things because others want them. Amit thinks that habit drives choices like marriage and children more than people realise.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Asked which Seen and the Unseen conversations changed him most.
recommendations.reason: His account of how moving to very long conversations changed the show and made him a better listener.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Suggested starting points for The Seen and the Unseen.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

recommendations.reason: Even if you don't care about hiking, it covers the two traps to avoid: competitiveness and treating life as a performance.

core_ideas.concept: People are brains, not stomachs
core_ideas.explanation: Amit rejects the idea of overpopulation outright. The right population is whatever arises through consent and without coercion. People move from low-density places to high-density cities, which are also the most prosperous places, so they are voting with their feet. Treating people as mouths to feed is condescending. They are minds that create value.
core_ideas.quote: There is no such thing as overpopulation. People are brains, not stomachs.

core_ideas.concept: Low fertility, pension traps, and India's north-south buffer
core_ideas.explanation: Young people bring energy, risk-taking and dynamism. Ageing societies make better films but face more social problems. The deeper danger is badly designed state pension systems that go bankrupt when the ratio of young to old shifts. India has a temporary cushion: free migration from the north supports the ageing south. When the north and east age too, the gap with the south and west will become a much bigger problem. Amit adds that immigration is the ultimate fix for ageing.
core_ideas.quote: So for a generation or so, the aging south is supported by enormous migration flows from the North.

core_ideas.concept: How India lost garment exports to Bangladesh
core_ideas.explanation: Only about 35% of working-age Indians are employed, one of the worst rates in the world. With so many idle workers, wages should fall, but high minimum wages and dense labour laws make large workforces risky to employ, so firms stay small. Bangladesh avoided this, has lower wages, and attracts factories from all over the world. West Bengal's trade-union troubles add to the contrast. Garment work is low-end and labour-intensive, so this was India's game to lose.
core_ideas.quote: So India has a self-inflicted wound of an artificially low working population and artificially small economy because the Indian state has damaged the ability of the labor market to function.

core_ideas.concept: Growth for poverty, market-failure tools for the environment
core_ideas.explanation: India's PPP-adjusted income per person is about a tenth of America's, so degrowth is morally wrong here. Amit calls it a classic luxury belief. Ajay separates the problems blamed on capitalism. Low wages and poor working conditions get fixed by growth: a poor factory is hot, a richer one adds fans, and a richer one still adds air conditioning. Pollution, carbon emissions and the loss of biodiversity are externalities. They call for taxes, Coasean bargains or state action, not for slower growth.
core_ideas.quote: I think that for a country at the poverty levels of India, degrowth is just morally wrong.

core_ideas.concept: Funding should follow the child
core_ideas.explanation: There is no single Indian education template. Kerala, Himachal and UP are on different paths. Large parts of India have already moved to private schools, yet public money flows only to pupils in state schools. Ajay calls that mean and unfair, and argues the state's job is to route public money fairly, for example through vouchers.
core_ideas.quote: it's better to have the funding follow the child.

core_ideas.concept: The one price a market economy lets the central bank set
core_ideas.explanation: Asked how a believer in prices for everything can accept a central bank fixing short-term interest rates, Ajay answers from first principles. Money solves the double-coincidence-of-wants problem that makes barter hopeless at scale. In a fiat system, the only known way to create money requires the central bank to pick that short rate. Crypto offers a possible route to money without the state, which he takes seriously.
core_ideas.quote: And the only recipe we know to make money involves the central bank picking a number for the interest rate at the short end.

core_ideas.concept: Organisations versus institutions
core_ideas.explanation: In India, 'institution' is used too loosely. An institution behaves predictably and consistently no matter who is in charge, which brings it close to the rule of law. Hindustan Lever qualifies. Most Indian state bodies are personalised organisations. RBI had to have inflation targeting written into law before it could become an institution. Organisations should be analysed sceptically, using public choice theory: people respond to incentives and seek ease, money and power.
core_ideas.quote: An institution is an impersonal capability. That people come and people go, but the institution works in a predictable and consistent way.

core_ideas.concept: Why Indian infrastructure is slow: good delays and bad ones
core_ideas.explanation: Some delay is healthy. Public debate about trade-offs and due process in land acquisition are what civilised countries do. The bad delay comes from incompetence, especially the government's weak contract management: market surveys, bid preparation, disputes and design changes. Private builders have improved a lot. A Bombay building that once took five to ten years now takes about two, and L&T builds airports abroad.
core_ideas.quote: This is a huge choke point in Indian state capacity, in Indian state capability.

core_ideas.concept: Reach and revenue
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's framework for the creator economy. Some work builds reach, which builds credibility, and revenue eventually comes from somewhere. For him the podcast is reach and the writing course pays. Early students came because of his podcast and blog; now they come through word of mouth. That only works if you put your heart into everything, not just the paid parts.
core_ideas.quote: you have to think of what you do in terms of two Rs. One is reach and one is revenue.

core_ideas.concept: Own your readers: start a newsletter
core_ideas.explanation: Waiting for newspapers to publish you means writing rarely, within fixed word counts and news cycles, with your readers scattered. A newsletter lets you write more often, iterate toward excellence and choose your own form. Every reader who likes a piece subscribes, so you build a community you own. Amit gives this advice to any writer, especially in India, where outlets for long-form journalism are scarce.
core_ideas.quote: That email database belongs to you, not to a Substack or to any other newsletter site.

core_ideas.concept: There is no objectively great book, only the right book at the right time
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that we change over time, so a book's impact depends on when it reaches us. The skill is to engage lightly with many books and keep a mental index of what each one covers, so the right one can land when you are ready. Amit agrees: reading a hundred books indiscriminately beats reading ten selected ones, and you should reach for a book, not your phone, when you're bored.
core_ideas.quote: And what we need is the matching process where the right book shows up at the right time.

core_ideas.concept: Your hours build your future self
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's recipe for breadth: cut distractions with hard limits (his phone greys out Twitter and Instagram after half an hour each), read a lot, take notes, and file Twitter bookmarks into folders to revisit later. Every hour either makes your future self smarter or duller. Willpower is a muscle that strengthens with use. He also defends rest: John Lennon's line that no time is wasted unless you feel it is wasted.
core_ideas.quote: You play Candy Crush for an hour, your future self is stupider than they would otherwise be and you read a book for an hour, you are making your future self smarter.

core_ideas.concept: Purpose, community and adjacencies: the engine of a life of knowledge
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay adds four points. Deliberately step back from mass culture like cricket, Bollywood and TV. Invest in your five, fifteen or fifty people, because conversation fuels learning. Avoid running on mid-level goals like getting a job or becoming famous. Treat everything as relevant instead of becoming a narrow specialist. Memory works by connection, so the more your knowledge links up, the more you retain, and you move into new fields one adjacent step at a time. His own purpose, which he can control even when the wider world goes wrong, is to build knowledge and community.
core_ideas.quote: life is too long to run on such middle level goals. So purpose is the ultimate superpower

core_ideas.concept: Learn India by looking out of the window
core_ideas.explanation: India is not a subject you learn from a single textbook, the way you might learn physics. You are surrounded by the source material, so observe it with curiosity. Ajay's example is how the gender mix of flights changes with the time of day. Keep asking why things are the way they are.
core_ideas.quote: So intellectualize about what you see rather than experiencing the day in a state of deadness.

core_ideas.concept: Spontaneous order produces bad things too, and also fixes them
core_ideas.explanation: A listener argues that patriarchy and caste also emerged through spontaneous order. Amit agrees the term is descriptive, not a claim that the outcome is good. Ajay says not to expect utopia: global warming is a market failure that calls for state action, while social evils have to be changed from the bottom up by society itself. Amit adds that the world has become far better for women over a century, through changing values and markets, not through lazy calls to pass another law.
core_ideas.quote: Whatever is imposed from the top, partly it doesn't work too well and partly it is truly dangerous because who knows what the values and the culture of the people at the top are.

core_ideas.concept: National development versus 'kinky' development
core_ideas.explanation: Asked about intellectual dishonesty in economics, Amit draws on Lant Pritchett's distinction. National development asks the hard, messy question of how to end poverty. 'Kinky' development tackles small questions with neat answers that advance careers but barely touch the problem. Amit names RCTs as the classic example.
core_ideas.quote: you can choose to ignore it and go for what he calls kinky development, where you tackle much smaller questions at a much smaller level, which have easy answers which get you career advancement and which don't make any dent on the problem.

core_ideas.concept: Profit is philanthropy, within limits
core_ideas.explanation: Amit says Nehru was wrong to tell J.R.D. Tata that profit is a dirty word. In a competitive market, every trade leaves both sides better off, a 'double thank you'. Like individuals under Mill's harm principle, firms may do as they please unless they harm others, for example by colluding with the state. Ajay adds that in India, where a malfunctioning state lets firms legally impose costs on others, an ethical business is one that stays aware of the market failures it causes.
core_ideas.quote: Profit is not a dirty word in a competitive marketplace. You're making someone better off. It is the highest form of philanthropy.

core_ideas.concept: Freedom feels unintuitive
core_ideas.explanation: Our minds were shaped in prehistoric times, so we think tribally and top-down, and our first reaction to behaviour we dislike is to ban it, even when it harms no one. We see the world as zero-sum and miss that trade is positive-sum. That is why freedom is undervalued as a core value in India.
core_ideas.quote: We think of the world in zero sum ways.

core_ideas.concept: Market failure is rare; government failure is everywhere
core_ideas.explanation: The one place Amit and Ajay part ways. Ajay often justifies state action by pointing to market failure. Amit worries that people hear this as 'market failure is everywhere', when in fact it is rare and government failure is built into the state's incentives. Their values on freedom, autonomy and consent are fully aligned. Amit also notes that friendship rests on shared values, not identical views.
core_ideas.quote: market failures are incredibly rare. Government failure is ubiquitous.

core_ideas.concept: Praise effort, not attributes
core_ideas.explanation: Based on the Mueller and Dweck experiment, Amit's top parenting advice is to praise children for trying, not for being clever. Children told they are smart came to feel entitled, eased off and even cheated. Amit thinks it happened to him: as a young man he was full of himself and didn't try hard enough.
core_ideas.quote: I simply wish that I had never thought I was intelligent and I had only assumed that I must try, try, try harder and harder and harder.

core_ideas.concept: Technology adds magnitude to whatever you already are
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's biggest change of mind. He used to believe Moore's Law, Unix and the internet would make the world better by spreading knowledge. Now he sees them as amplifiers. Power makes you more of what you already are, so for some people technology helps and for others it makes things more toxic. Amit thinks the dark side is real but that technology, including AI, is still a large net positive.
core_ideas.quote: And if there was good values and good character inside you, then the CPUs and the internet have taken that vector and added magnitude to that vector.

core_ideas.concept: Three behaviours to denormalise
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay names three. First, careless noise: motorcycles, construction, speakerphones, wedding parties you can hear a kilometre away. Second, celebrity culture, which reveres people famous for being famous. Third, populist contempt for expertise: fifty years ago people knew less but respected knowledge. Amit adds a fourth: judge people's virtue by what they do, not what they say. He notes that feminists who have worked in the field for decades complain about younger activists who win status on Twitter through slogans without doing the work.
core_ideas.quote: today the person without the knowledge armed with the WhatsApp is cocky and says, I look down on the people who have knowledge.

core_ideas.concept: Mimetic desire, communities of choice, and rooted cosmopolitanism
core_ideas.explanation: Before marrying or having children, ask whether you want it or just copy others (René Girard's mimetic desire). Choose your community by values and interests, not by the circumstances of your birth. Amit's own regret, using a phrase from Sugata Srinivasaraju: he became cosmopolitan without staying rooted in his own culture, and not everything about where we come from is toxic. In the end, what matters is the people you collect.
core_ideas.quote: I think that I am cosmopolitan but I'm not rooted enough. And that is a lament that I have.

core_ideas.concept: Two traps to drop: competition and performance
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's answer to how a young person should find meaning. Stop trying to outdo classmates and neighbours, and stop living for social media or your résumé. Once both are gone, you are left doing what you actually value. He links this to his calm: someone who isn't competing or performing doesn't rattle easily.
core_ideas.quote: And the second is stop this business of life as a performance that I'm doing things because I can put them up on social media or I will burnish my resume and then I will look good in the eyes of others.

core_ideas.concept: Pick one, and find a master
core_ideas.explanation: Many young people are paralysed by possibilities and end up doing nothing. Amit's cure is Steve Jobs's advice to Jony Ive: learn to say no even to things you love, then commit to one and let flow come. Ajay adds that apprenticing with a passionate master, not chasing credentials, teaches the craft and gives you energy.
core_ideas.quote: Stop daydreaming. Pick one. Immerse yourself in it. Love the doing of it.

core_ideas.concept: Be the best you can be at time T
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's new rule is to end every year fitter than the last and with more work done. Ajay pushes back: ageing is certain, so that target sets you up for sadness. A better aim is to be the best version of yourself at each point in time, without raging against the limits age brings.
core_ideas.quote: I want to be the best Amit Varma I can be at time T.

core_ideas.concept: 1947 came at an unlucky moment
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's single wish from a genie: India's founding generation was formed between 1927 and 1947, when freedom was in retreat worldwide and war economies made full state mobilisation look normal. He would send Nehru, Gandhi, Rajagopalachari and others a bag of books. Ideally, the new state would have spent about 10% of GDP on basic public goods: rule of law, courts and a fair tax system. Amit doubts books alone would have changed minds formed over decades.
core_ideas.quote: I feel that we just got very, very unlucky in the great freedom movement generation, where I think 1947 was an unlucky year.

core_ideas.concept: Caste: thousands of small populations, slowly dissolved by markets
core_ideas.explanation: Caste endogamy, enforced for about 2,000 years, turned India into many small, closed gene pools. That shrinks economic networks, limits mobility, and causes diseases found nowhere else. Amit's answer, echoing Chandra Bhan Prasad, whose two heroes are Babasaheb Ambedkar and Adam Smith, is growth and cities. When firms compete for workers and customers, discrimination becomes costly. The 1991 reforms freed many lower-caste people from old constraints, though Amit admits the fight is far from over.
core_ideas.quote: If you're looking for a large population, look at the Han Chinese. But India is really a collection of thousands of small populations.

core_ideas.concept: Metcalfe's law and the rise of English
core_ideas.explanation: Among the elite, English has become India's common language. By Metcalfe's law, a network's value grows with the square of its nodes, so every new English speaker makes the network more valuable, and parents know it. On the street, Hinglish has won. Against this flattening, the long tail of dialects survives online.
core_ideas.quote: Parents have got the memo and are pushing their kids into learning more and more English.

core_ideas.concept: Universal suffrage is non-negotiable
core_ideas.explanation: Asked whether voting could be limited to people who pass a test, Amit says no. Education doesn't guarantee good judgement, and whoever sets the bar decides who is left out. India gave women the vote before many rich nations did, and he counts universal suffrage among the things the republic got right.
core_ideas.quote: My point is the moment you create a bar, somebody decides what that bar is, and people are left out of the process.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: After Ajay explains how dehydration makes the heart work harder, Amit says: 'The Bengali in me is freaking delighted because I'm just thinking that I don't need to go running anymore. I can just stay away from water and walk around gently and the heart is still working for you.' Ajay replies: 'More challenging than walking around gently when well hydrated.'

Ajay's theory of cinema: 'the quality of movies in a country is basically proportional to the median age. So when India was a very young country, the quality of the movies was atrocious.' He later concludes that young people 'give us bad movies' but are great for society. Amit responds by recommending Wild Strawberries.

Ajay asks whether, once he has made Amit a master programmer, Amit would cry at a beautiful algorithm. Amit: 'Tears are coming to my eyes thinking of the amount of brute coercion that would be required to make me a master of computer programming.'
Ajay's rental tip in his rant against noise: 'never rent a house that is close to a temple or a mosque because they'll just make so much noise.'

Halfway through explaining the Dweck experiment, Amit stops to report that someone below is selling aloo pyaaz, offers some, and adds as a keto aside that aloo is heavy on carbs and pyaaz not so much.
Ajay says power makes you more of what you already are. Amit cuts in: 'Since power corrupts, then that means we're all inherently...'
Reading out a listener question from Vaishnav Vyas, who shoots the show: 'Vaishnav Vyas. I wonder who that is.' Amit: 'I wonder who that is.'

Amit on 'neoliberalism': it is only ever a curse word of the left, nobody calls themselves one, and 'whenever I hear someone using that term I automatically assume intellectual laziness... I lose respect for people who use that word.'

The Bir Sessions: this AMA is the first of ten episodes recorded in a week in Bir, Himachal Pradesh. Ajay came there at the end of a May hike in Himachal, his first big outing after a fracture in January.
Nehru's remark to J.R.D. Tata, 'Do not speak to me of profit. It is a dirty word', which Amit says Nehru got completely wrong.
Amit quotes Prem Panicker, a friend and Seen and the Unseen guest, who said that with beat reporters gone, Indian journalism is 'a mile wide and an inch deep'.
'No man can cross the same river twice': Ajay's line for why the same book can transform you at one age and fall flat at another.
'If you're not busy being born, you're busy dying': Amit applies it to the specialist who stops engaging with the world.
Annie Dillard: 'How you spend your days is, of course, how you spend your life.' Amit's answer to what his aim in life is.
Richard Bach: 'What a caterpillar calls the end of the world, the master calls a butterfly.' Amit adds it after Ajay's point about apprenticing with a master.
Steve Jobs's advice to Jony Ive when they first met in the 1990s, as Amit recalls it: learn to say no to the things you love.
'There will be no Ram Rajya': Ajay's reminder that no system, including spontaneous order, will deliver paradise.

Ajay loves Ramanujan as much as Einstein and Gandhi as much as Nehru, because for him 'it's the ascent of man', not ethnicity or a line on a map. Amit notes the phrase comes from Bronowski's book and suggests 'the Ascent of Humans' instead.
The Tatsinskaya airfield near Stalingrad: Ajay's example of a story he has known for 25 years but still fact-checked, down to the distances, before the maps episode.
